A lost connection ends the channel of every source and sink that uses it. Each
source reports a retryable error and opens a new channel on the next
`receive`, while each sink fails the completions still waiting for a
confirmation, which stops their subscriptions as described under
[publication](#publication).

The handle, the source, and the sink each have `validate`, which checks the
values without contacting the broker. The handle's `Debug` output hides the
URI's password.

The adapters declare no exchanges, queues, or bindings. Create the topology
with broker definitions, the management tools, or application code before the
subscription starts; a source whose queue does not exist fails its receive and
retries under the subscription's `receive_retry`.

The source's `prefetch` is the `basic.qos` prefetch count, 100 by default: the number of unacknowledged messages the broker sends ahead. It bounds
the source's buffered and in-flight deliveries together, so keep it at least as
large as the subscription's `max_in_flight`.

## Records

`RabbitMqRecord<T>` is the decoded input and `RabbitMqPublish<T>` the output.
The codec applies to the message body. AMQP has no null body, so the value is
always present and RabbitMQ records support no tombstones.

`headers` is the AMQP `headers` table as a map of `RabbitMqValue`, which keeps
each field's AMQP type: integers of each width, floats, decimals, timestamps,
booleans, nested arrays and tables, strings, and byte arrays. Short strings and
UTF-8 long strings are read as `String`, and a long string that is not UTF-8 as
`Bytes`. `RabbitMqProperties` holds the basic properties applications set:
content type and encoding, priority, correlation ID, reply-to, expiration,
message ID, timestamp, type (`kind`), user ID, and app ID. The protocol limits
text properties, header names, and routing keys to 255 bytes; `prepare` rejects
longer values.

`RabbitMqMetadata` contains read-only delivery facts: the consumed queue, the
exchange and routing key the message was published with, the redelivered flag,
whether the message is persistent, and its delivery tag. `RabbitMqPublish` has
none of them, so the sink publishes to its configured exchange with the output's
routing key or the configured one, and input metadata is never inherited
implicitly.

The raw form of a `RabbitMqMessage` is a `RabbitMqRecord<Vec<u8>>` with the
undecoded body. Dead letters carry it, so the original body, headers,
properties, and delivery metadata survive even when decoding fails.

## Acknowledgements and ordering

The source consumes with manual acknowledgements. A successful ACK sends
`basic.ack` for the delivery's tag. AMQP does not confirm an acknowledgement,
so a connection lost right after it can still requeue the message, which is
then processed again. Dropping a `RabbitMqMessage` leaves its message
unacknowledged until its channel closes, when the broker requeues it with the
redelivered flag set; this happens when the source closes or loses its
channel or connection.

A delivery tag is valid only on the channel that delivered it. When the
connection or channel is lost, or the broker cancels the consumer, `receive`
cancels the revocation token of every delivery of that channel and reports a
retryable error, and the next `receive` connects again. The runtime abandons
revoked deliveries without ACK or subscription failure, because the broker has
already requeued them. An acknowledgement that finds its channel closed also
revokes its channel's deliveries and fails. Broker heartbeats detect a silent
connection loss.

RabbitMQ delivers a queue's messages to one consumer in order, but distributes
them among several consumers and requeues unacknowledged messages, so
deliveries have no ordering key by default and run in parallel up to the
subscription's `concurrency`. Set the source's `ordered` to give every
delivery the queue as its ordering key, so that `ProcessingOrder::PerKey`
processes one message at a time in delivery order. Combine it with a queue that
has a single active consumer (`x-single-active-consumer`) for order across
application instances; a requeued message is still delivered again after later
ones.

The consumer is a stream fed by the connection's I/O task: a delivery leaves it
only when a receive completes, so dropping a pending receive does not consume a
delivery.

## Publication

`prepare` encodes the value and converts the routing key, headers, and
properties to their AMQP form once, so publish retries reuse them. The sink
opens a channel in publisher-confirm mode on the handle's publishing connection
on first use, and again after the previous channel or its connection was lost.

`RabbitMqSink::submit` returns once the message is written to the channel, with
a completion that resolves on the broker's publisher confirmation. The runtime
frees the job's concurrency slot at submission and acknowledges the input when
the confirmation arrives. `publish` writes the message and waits for its
confirmation. A broker `nack`, a channel lost before the confirmation, or a
message returned as unroutable fails the completion, which stops the
subscription without acknowledging the input, and the input is redelivered.

The sink's `mandatory`, enabled by default, asks the broker to return
a message no queue receives, so a missing binding fails the subscription
instead of losing outputs. Disable it to let the broker discard such messages.
`persistent`, also enabled by default, publishes with the persistent delivery
mode, so durable queues keep the messages across a broker restart; the
confirmation then arrives after the broker has written them.

`max_pending` bounds the messages submitted to one sink whose confirmation has
not arrived; the default is 1000. `submit` waits while that
many are outstanding. Messages on one channel are confirmed in publication
order. `close` stops new submissions, waits for outstanding confirmations, and
closes the sink's channel. The publishing connection stays open for the
handle's other sinks.

## Metadata inheritance

Register `RabbitMqInherit` on a RabbitMQ-to-RabbitMQ subscription to forward the
received headers and the properties that describe the payload or its
conversation: content type, content encoding, type, correlation ID, app ID, and
priority.

```rust,ignore
use beavers::adapters::rabbitmq::RabbitMqInherit;

Subscription::new("orders", rabbitmq_source, rabbitmq_sink, handler)
    .middleware(RabbitMqInherit::new())
```

Explicit output fields take precedence: a received header is added only when the
output does not set that name, and a property only when the output leaves it
`None`. Dead-letter headers starting with `beavers-dlq-` are never inherited.
The message ID, timestamp, expiration, reply-to address, and user ID identify or
address one message and are never inherited, and neither is the routing key, so
an output cannot route back to the queue it came from unless the sink is
configured to. `without_headers()` and `without_properties()` disable either
part.

A handler that returns a plain value between a RabbitMQ source and sink gets
`RabbitMqInherit::new()` automatically. See the
[runtime guide](../runtime/handlers.md#handler-shapes). Register
`TraceContext` after `RabbitMqInherit` to replace inherited trace-context
headers; the source reads trace context from string headers.

## Dead letters

`RabbitMqPublish::from_dead_letter` forwards a dead letter with its original
body, headers, and properties, adding string headers with the failure details
and the queue, exchange, and routing key of its first receipt.
`RabbitMqDeadLetter::from_record` reads them back; see
[forwarding dead letters](../runtime/errors.md#forwarding-dead-letters-to-a-broker-topic).
The sink's routing key applies, so a sink on the default exchange whose routing
key names a dead-letter queue collects them there.

RabbitMQ's own dead-lettering, through a queue's dead-letter exchange, applies
to messages that are rejected, expire, or exceed a queue's delivery limit. The
adapter never rejects a message, so the subscription's error policy decides
what happens to a failed delivery. On a quorum queue, a delivery limit
(`x-delivery-limit`) with a dead-letter exchange still moves a message that
keeps being requeued, for example because it crashes the process every time,
out of the queue.

## Delivery guarantees

A source ACK and a sink publication are separate operations, and AMQP
acknowledgements are not confirmed, so a failure between them, or a connection
loss right after an acknowledgement, can produce a duplicate on redelivery. The
adapter does not use AMQP transactions; RabbitMQ pipelines are at-least-once.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/adapters/sqs.md -->

# SQS adapter

The optional `sqs` feature provides typed Amazon SQS source and sink adapters
backed by the AWS SDK for Rust (`aws-sdk-sqs`).

```toml
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["sqs"] }
```

## Configuration

An `Sqs` handle holds how the adapter reaches SQS. `region`, `endpoint_url`,
and `credentials` are optional builder methods on it: unset, the SDK's default
chains resolve the region and credentials from the environment, shared
configuration files, web identity, or container and instance metadata. Set
`endpoint_url` to use an SQS-compatible emulator such as ElasticMQ or
LocalStack. `SqsCredentials::new` takes an access key ID and secret access key;
the `Debug` output of `SqsCredentials` hides the secret key and session token.

`handle.source::<C>(queue_url)` and `handle.sink::<C>(queue_url)` build a
source and a sink for one queue; `source_with_codec` and `sink_with_codec` take
a codec value as their first argument instead of using the codec's default. A
URL ending in `.fifo` names a FIFO queue.

```rust
use beavers::{Utf8, adapters::sqs::{Sqs, SqsPublish}};

let sqs = Sqs::new().region("eu-west-1");
let source = sqs.source::<Utf8>(
    "https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/orders",
);
let sink = sqs.sink::<Utf8>(
    "https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/processed-orders.fifo",
);

let output = SqsPublish::new("created".to_owned()).with_message_group_id("customer-7");
```

All sources and sinks built from one handle share one SDK client, with its
credential provider and HTTP connection pool. The client is created on the
first `receive` or publication of any of them, which also validates the
settings. Each builder method on the handle returns a handle with a client of
its own, so configure the handle before building sources and sinks from it.
The handle, the source, and the sink each have `validate`, which checks the
values without contacting AWS.

The adapters create no queues and set no queue attributes such as a redrive
policy. Create them with infrastructure tooling before the subscription starts.

The source receives with long polling. Its `max_messages` (1 to 10, default
10) is the batch size of each `ReceiveMessage` call and `wait_time`
(at most 20 seconds, the default) how long a call waits for messages.
`visibility_timeout`, 30 seconds by default, is requested with every receive and
overrides the queue's own default.

## Records

`SqsRecord<T>` is the decoded input and `SqsPublish<T>` the output. The codec
applies to the message body. SQS has no null body, so the value is always
present and SQS records support no tombstones. SQS bodies are text: `prepare`
rejects an encoded value that is not UTF-8, so binary codecs such as Protobuf
and Avro need a text representation, such as the
[`Base64` wrapper](../codecs/wrappers/base64.md), before they can be sent.

`attributes` holds the message attributes as `SqsAttributeValue::String`,
`Number` in its decimal text form, or `Binary`. A custom type label such as
`Number.float` is read as its base type and not published again. SQS accepts at
most 10 attributes per message.

`SqsMetadata` contains read-only facts about a received message: the queue URL,
message ID, receive count, sent and first-receive timestamps, and for FIFO
queues the message group, deduplication ID, and sequence number. `SqsPublish`
has none of them except the FIFO message group and deduplication ID, which the
output sets itself, and an optional delivery `delay`.

The raw form of an `SqsMessage` is an `SqsRecord<Vec<u8>>` with the undecoded
body. Dead letters carry it, so the original body, attributes, and metadata
survive even when decoding fails.

## Acknowledgements and ordering

A received message stays invisible to other consumers for the visibility
timeout. The source keeps every message it has received and not yet deleted
invisible: a background task extends a message's visibility with
`ChangeMessageVisibilityBatch` once a third of its timeout has passed, until it
is acknowledged or released. SQS limits visibility to 12 hours from the receipt;
a message held longer becomes visible again.

A successful ACK deletes the message with `DeleteMessage`, retried under the
source's `ack_retry`. Dropping an `SqsMessage` without acknowledging it,
or closing the source, changes the visibility of its remaining messages to zero,
so another receive takes them at once with an incremented receive count.

A receipt handle is valid only for the receipt that returned it. When an
extension fails or arrives too late, SQS may already have handed the message to
another consumer, so the adapter cancels that delivery's revocation token. The
runtime abandons a revoked delivery without ACK or subscription failure. An
acknowledgement that finds its visibility expired, or that SQS rejects as an
invalid receipt handle, also revokes the delivery and fails.

A standard queue delivers messages in no particular order, so its deliveries
have no ordering key and run in parallel up to the subscription's
`concurrency`. A FIFO queue delivers each message group in order; each delivery's
ordering key is its message group, so `ProcessingOrder::PerKey` processes one
message per group at a time while groups run in parallel.

`ReceiveMessage` runs as a task the source keeps: dropping a pending `receive`
leaves the call running, and the next `receive` takes its messages.

## Publication

`prepare` encodes the value and converts the attributes once, so publish
retries reuse them. It requires a message group ID for a FIFO queue, rejects a
per-message delay there because FIFO queues accept only a queue-wide delay, and
limits the delay to 15 minutes elsewhere. A FIFO queue without content-based
deduplication also needs `deduplication_id`.

`SqsSink::publish` sends the message with `SendMessage` and succeeds once SQS
has stored it. The SDK retries throttling and transient errors itself.
Parameter errors such as an invalid attribute fail as `PublishRejected`, which
the subscription's error policy can dead-letter instead of retrying. The sink
keeps no pending messages, so `close` only stops new publications.

## Metadata inheritance

Register `SqsInherit` on an SQS-to-SQS subscription to forward the received
message attributes:

```rust,ignore
use beavers::adapters::sqs::SqsInherit;

Subscription::new("orders", sqs_source, sqs_sink, handler)
    .middleware(SqsInherit::new().with_message_group())
```

A received attribute is added only when the output does not set that name, and
dead-letter attributes starting with `beavers-dlq-` are never inherited.
`with_message_group()` also forwards the FIFO message group when the output
leaves it `None`, for pipelines between FIFO queues. The message ID,
deduplication ID, and delay are never inherited. `without_attributes()`
disables attribute inheritance.

A handler that returns a plain value between an SQS source and sink gets
`SqsInherit::new()` automatically; register
`SqsInherit::new().with_message_group()` explicitly to forward groups. See the
[runtime guide](../runtime/handlers.md#handler-shapes). Register
`TraceContext` after `SqsInherit` to replace inherited trace-context
attributes; the source reads trace context from string attributes.

## Dead letters

`SqsPublish::from_dead_letter` forwards a dead letter with its original body,
attributes, and FIFO message group. Because SQS accepts at most 10 attributes,
the failure details and the URL and message ID of the first receipt are written
as one JSON object into the `beavers-dlq-details` string attribute; a message
that already has 10 attributes is rejected by SQS. `SqsDeadLetter::from_record`
reads them back; see
[forwarding dead letters](../runtime/errors.md#forwarding-dead-letters-to-a-broker-topic).

A queue's redrive policy moves a message to its dead-letter queue after
`maxReceiveCount` receives without deletion. The subscription's error policy
decides what happens to a failed delivery first, so the redrive policy applies
to messages that are received again and again without being acknowledged, for
example because they crash the process every time. Keep `maxReceiveCount` high
enough that the releases of a source's shutdowns do not exhaust it.

## Delivery guarantees

A source ACK and a sink publication are separate requests, so a failure between
them, or a visibility timeout that expires before the deletion, can produce a
duplicate. Standard queues may also deliver a message more than once. SQS
pipelines are at-least-once; FIFO deduplication applies only to messages sent
within its five-minute window.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/adapters/pubsub.md -->

# Pub/Sub adapter

The optional `pubsub` feature provides typed Google Cloud Pub/Sub source and
sink adapters backed by the official Google Cloud client library for Rust
(`google-cloud-pubsub`).

```toml
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["pubsub"] }
```

## Configuration

A `PubSub` handle holds the connection settings that its sources and sinks
share. It resolves its credentials once and keeps one subscriber client for all
of its sources. Each sink has a publisher client of its own, because a Pub/Sub
publisher batches messages for one topic, and uses the handle's credentials.
Credentials and clients are created on the first `receive` or publication that
needs them, which also validates the settings.

The handle uses Application Default Credentials unless `anonymous()` is set:
the `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` key file, the gcloud user credentials, or
the metadata server of the Google Cloud environment the application runs in.
`endpoint` replaces `https://pubsub.googleapis.com`, for example with a
regional endpoint. Each handle builder method returns a handle with
credentials and clients of its own, so configure the handle before building
sources and sinks from it.

`source` takes the full name of one subscription,
`projects/{project}/subscriptions/{id}`, and `sink` the full name of one topic,
`projects/{project}/topics/{id}`. `source_with_codec` and `sink_with_codec`
take a codec value first. The handle, source, and sink each have `validate`,
which checks the values without contacting Google Cloud.

```rust
use beavers::{Utf8, adapters::pubsub::{PubSub, PubSubPublish}};

let pubsub = PubSub::new();
let source = pubsub.source::<Utf8>("projects/my-project/subscriptions/orders");
let sink = pubsub.sink::<Utf8>("projects/my-project/topics/processed-orders");

let output = PubSubPublish::new("created".to_owned()).with_ordering_key("customer-7");
```

For the [Pub/Sub emulator](../development.md#broker-configuration), set the
endpoint to its address and send no credentials:
`PubSub::new().endpoint("http://localhost:8085").anonymous()`.

The adapters create no topics or subscriptions and set no subscription
properties such as message ordering, exactly-once delivery, or a dead-letter
policy. Create them with infrastructure tooling before the subscription starts.

The source receives through one streaming pull. Pub/Sub stops sending once
`max_outstanding_messages` (1000 by default) messages or
`max_outstanding_bytes` (100 MiB) of data are received and not yet
acknowledged; zero or less sets no limit. The runtime's `max_in_flight` bounds
the deliveries it holds; the rest of the outstanding messages wait in the
client's buffer with their leases extended.

The sink's `batch_delay`, 10 milliseconds by default, is how long the client
collects outputs into one `Publish` request.

```rust
use beavers::{Utf8, adapters::pubsub::PubSub};
use std::time::Duration;

let pubsub = PubSub::new();
let source = pubsub
    .source::<Utf8>("projects/my-project/subscriptions/orders")
    .max_outstanding_messages(200)
    .ack_deadline(Duration::from_secs(120));
let sink = pubsub
    .sink::<Utf8>("projects/my-project/topics/processed-orders")
    .batch_delay(Duration::from_millis(50));
```

## Records

`PubSubRecord<T>` is the decoded input and `PubSubPublish<T>` the output. The
codec applies to the message data. Pub/Sub has no null message, so the value
is always present and Pub/Sub records support no tombstones. The data is bytes,
so every codec works.

`attributes` holds the message attributes as strings. `ordering_key` is the key
the message was published with, or `None`. `PubSubMetadata` contains read-only
facts about a received message: the subscription, message ID, publish time in
milliseconds since the Unix epoch, and the delivery attempt, which Pub/Sub
counts only on a subscription with a dead-letter policy. `PubSubPublish` has
none of them; it sets the value, attributes, and ordering key.

The raw form of a `PubSubMessage` is a `PubSubRecord<Vec<u8>>` with the
undecoded data. Dead letters carry it, so the original data, attributes,
ordering key, and metadata survive even when decoding fails.

## Acknowledgements and ordering

Pub/Sub redelivers a message whose acknowledgement deadline passes. The client
extends the lease of every message the source has received and not yet
acknowledged, by `ack_deadline` (60 seconds by default, 10 seconds to 10
minutes) at a time, for at most `max_lease` (one hour by default). When a
delivery is still held at `max_lease`, the source cancels its revocation
token, because the client stops extending it and Pub/Sub will redeliver it.
The runtime abandons a revoked delivery without ACK or subscription failure.

An ACK hands the acknowledgement to the client, which sends acknowledgements in
batches without confirmation, so an acknowledged message can still be
redelivered. On a subscription with exactly-once delivery, the ACK waits for
Pub/Sub to confirm it, fails when the client cannot confirm it, and revokes the
delivery when its lease expired first. Dropping a `PubSubMessage` without
acknowledging it nacks it, so Pub/Sub redelivers it at once.

`close` stops the stream, waits until the deliveries the source handed out are
acknowledged or dropped, sends the pending acknowledgements, and nacks the
messages the client received but the source never handed out. A stream that
fails with an error the client does not retry itself is replaced on the next
`receive`; deliveries from the failed stream keep their leases until they
finish.

A message published with an ordering key has the subscription and that key as
its ordering key, so `ProcessingOrder::PerKey` processes one message per key at
a time while keys run in parallel. Pub/Sub delivers the messages of a key in
order only on a subscription with message ordering enabled. Messages without an
ordering key have no ordering key and run in parallel up to the subscription's
`concurrency`.

The client buffers what the stream received, so a cancelled `receive` loses no
message.

## Publication

`prepare` encodes the value and checks Pub/Sub's limits once, so publish
retries reuse the message: at most 100 attributes, names of 1 to 256 bytes that
do not start with `goog`, values and the ordering key of at most 1024 bytes,
and data or at least one attribute.

`PubSubSink::publish` succeeds once Pub/Sub has stored the message and returned
its ID. The client batches publications and retries transient errors itself.
An invalid argument fails as `PublishRejected`, which the subscription's error
policy can dead-letter instead of retrying. After a publication with an
ordering key fails, the client pauses that key; the sink resumes it, so the
runtime's retry or a later output of the key can be published. `close` sends
the batched messages and stops new publications.

## Metadata inheritance

Register `PubSubInherit` on a Pub/Sub-to-Pub/Sub subscription to forward the
received message attributes:

```rust,ignore
use beavers::adapters::pubsub::PubSubInherit;

Subscription::new("orders", pubsub_source, pubsub_sink, handler)
    .middleware(PubSubInherit::new().with_ordering_key())
```

A received attribute is added only when the output does not set that name, and
dead-letter attributes starting with `beavers-dlq-` are never inherited.
`with_ordering_key()` also forwards the ordering key when the output leaves it
`None`. The message ID, publish time, and delivery attempt are never inherited.
`without_attributes()` disables attribute inheritance.

A handler that returns a plain value between a Pub/Sub source and sink gets
`PubSubInherit::new()` automatically; register
`PubSubInherit::new().with_ordering_key()` explicitly to forward ordering keys.
See the [runtime guide](../runtime/handlers.md#handler-shapes). Register `TraceContext`
after `PubSubInherit` to replace inherited trace-context attributes; the source
reads trace context from attributes.

## Dead letters

`PubSubPublish::from_dead_letter` forwards a dead letter with its original
data, attributes, and ordering key, and adds the failure details and the
subscription and message ID of the first receipt as `beavers-dlq-*`
attributes. Pub/Sub limits attribute values to 1024 bytes, so a longer error
message is cut at a character boundary. `PubSubDeadLetter::from_record` reads
them back; see
[forwarding dead letters](../runtime/errors.md#forwarding-dead-letters-to-a-broker-topic).

A subscription's dead-letter policy moves a message to its dead-letter topic
after `maxDeliveryAttempts` deliveries without acknowledgement. The
subscription's error policy decides what happens to a failed delivery first,
so the dead-letter policy applies to messages that are delivered again and
again without being acknowledged, for example because they crash the process
every time. Keep `maxDeliveryAttempts` high enough that the nacks of a
source's shutdowns do not exhaust it.

## Delivery guarantees

A source ACK and a sink publication are separate requests, so a failure between
them, a lease that expires before the acknowledgement, or an acknowledgement
the client loses can produce a duplicate. Pub/Sub pipelines are at-least-once.
Exactly-once delivery on the input subscription confirms each acknowledgement
but does not make publication and acknowledgement atomic.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/adapters/servicebus.md -->

# Azure Service Bus adapter

The optional `servicebus` feature provides typed Azure Service Bus source and
sink adapters that speak AMQP 1.0 to a namespace through `fe2o3-amqp`.

```toml
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["servicebus"] }
```

## Configuration

A `ServiceBus` handle names a namespace, such as
`contoso.servicebus.windows.net`, and a credential:

- `shared_access_key(name, key)` signs a shared access signature for each
  entity the adapter uses and renews it before it expires.
- `shared_access_signature(token)` uses a token signed elsewhere. It cannot be
  renewed, so the connection fails once the token expires.

`ServiceBus::from_connection_string` reads a connection string as the Azure
portal and the Service Bus emulator show it. A connection string with
`EntityPath` is refused; pass the entity to the source or sink instead. The
`Debug` output of the handle hides the key and the signature.

The adapters connect with AMQP over TLS on port 5671 and authenticate with
claims-based security. `UseDevelopmentEmulator=true` in a connection string, or
`emulator()`, selects plain AMQP on port 5672 for the emulator; a port in the
namespace overrides either default. Microsoft Entra ID credentials are not
supported yet.

The handle opens one AMQP connection with one session, and every source and
sink built from it attaches its links to that session. Each entity is
authorized once on the connection through claims-based security, and tokens
signed with a shared access key are renewed before they expire. The connection
opens on the first use that needs it, which also validates the settings, and is
opened again after it is lost. Closing a source or sink detaches its links
only; the connection closes once the handle and every source and sink built
from it have been dropped. Each handle builder method returns a handle with a
connection of its own, so configure the handle before building sources and
sinks from it.

```rust
use beavers::{Utf8, adapters::servicebus::{ServiceBus, ServiceBusPublish}};

let bus = ServiceBus::from_connection_string(
    "Endpoint=sb://contoso.servicebus.windows.net/;SharedAccessKeyName=app;SharedAccessKey=...",
)?;
let source = bus.source::<Utf8>("orders/Subscriptions/billing");
let sink = bus.sink::<Utf8>("processed-orders");

let output = ServiceBusPublish::new("created".to_owned()).with_message_id("order-7");
# Ok::<(), beavers::Error>(())
```

`source` receives from a queue, a topic subscription written as
`{topic}/Subscriptions/{subscription}`, or a dead-letter subqueue such as
`orders/$DeadLetterQueue`. Session-enabled entities are not supported. The
source's `prefetch`, 10 by default, is how many messages Service Bus may send
ahead of `receive`. Each is locked from the moment it is sent, so keep
`prefetch` small enough that prefetched messages reach a handler well within
the lock duration.

`sink` sends to one queue or topic. The sink's `max_pending`, 1000 by default,
limits the messages sent and not yet accepted.

```rust
use beavers::{Utf8, adapters::servicebus::ServiceBus};

let bus = ServiceBus::new("contoso.servicebus.windows.net")
    .shared_access_key("app", "...");
let source = bus.source::<Utf8>("orders").prefetch(20);
let sink = bus.sink::<Utf8>("processed-orders").max_pending(100);
```

`source_with_codec` and `sink_with_codec` take a codec value first. The handle,
source, and sink each have `validate`, which checks the values without
contacting Service Bus. The adapters create no entities; create queues, topics,
subscriptions, and their rules with infrastructure tooling before the
subscription starts.

## Records

`ServiceBusRecord<T>` is the decoded input and `ServiceBusPublish<T>` the
output. The codec applies to the message body, which the adapters send as one
AMQP data section. A received message whose body is an AMQP value or sequence,
as some AMQP clients send, fails to decode; its raw form carries the AMQP
encoding of the body.

`application_properties` holds typed `ServiceBusValue`s: strings, booleans,
integers, floats, characters, timestamps, and UUIDs. Service Bus refuses binary
application properties and stores symbols as strings, so the adapter has
neither; received binary, decimal, and described values are skipped.

`ServiceBusProperties` holds the properties the sender sets: message ID,
correlation ID, session ID, reply-to address and session, subject, content type,
`to`, time to live, and partition key. `prepare` limits the identifiers to 128
characters, requires the partition key to equal a session ID when both are set,
and accepts a time to live from one millisecond to 49 days.

`ServiceBusMetadata` contains read-only facts about a received message: the
entity path, sequence number, enqueued and scheduled enqueue times in
milliseconds since the Unix epoch, delivery count, lock token, and the entity a
dead-lettered message came from. `ServiceBusPublish` has none of them except an
optional `scheduled_enqueue_time`, which keeps the message invisible until that
time.

The raw form of a `ServiceBusMessage` is a `ServiceBusRecord<Vec<u8>>` with the
undecoded body. Dead letters carry it, so the original body, properties, and
metadata survive even when decoding fails.

## Acknowledgements and ordering

The source receives in peek-lock mode. A received message is locked to the
source for the entity's lock duration. A background task renews the locks of
the messages the source has received and not yet settled with
`com.microsoft:renew-lock` once a third of the lock duration has passed, so a
handler may run longer than the lock duration.

A successful ACK completes the message with an `accepted` disposition. Service
Bus does not confirm a completion, so a completion sent just before the lock is
lost leaves the message to be delivered again. Dropping a `ServiceBusMessage`
without acknowledging it abandons the message, which Service Bus delivers again
at once with an incremented delivery count. Closing the source releases the
messages Service Bus sent ahead and the application never received, without
counting a delivery, and detaches its links; the handle's connection stays
open.

A lock that renewal reports lost, or that ends before it is renewed, means
Service Bus may already have handed the message to another receiver, so the
adapter cancels that delivery's revocation token. The runtime abandons a
revoked delivery without ACK or subscription failure. An ACK whose lock has
already ended also revokes the delivery and fails. When the connection or link
is lost, every unsettled delivery is revoked and the next `receive` attaches
again, reopening the handle's connection when it was lost.

Without sessions, Service Bus delivers messages in no guaranteed order, so the
deliveries have no ordering key and run in parallel up to the subscription's
`concurrency`.

`receive` is cancel-safe: a message that arrives for a dropped `receive` is
kept for the next one.

## Publication

`prepare` encodes the value and converts the properties once, so publish
retries reuse the message. `ServiceBusSink::submit` sends the message on the
link and returns a completion that resolves when Service Bus accepts it;
`publish` waits for that completion. A message larger than the link's maximum
message size fails as `PublishRejected`, which the subscription's error policy
can dead-letter instead of retrying. A lost connection fails the publication,
and the next one attaches again, reopening the handle's connection. `close`
stops new publications and detaches the send link; the handle's connection
stays open.

A scheduled message is stored at once, so a completed publication of a
scheduled message is as durable as any other.

## Metadata inheritance

Register `ServiceBusInherit` on a Service Bus to Service Bus subscription to
forward the received application properties:

```rust,ignore
use beavers::adapters::servicebus::ServiceBusInherit;

Subscription::new("orders", servicebus_source, servicebus_sink, handler)
    .middleware(ServiceBusInherit::new())
```

An application property is added only when the output does not set that name,
and dead-letter properties starting with `beavers-dlq-` are never inherited.
`with_session()` also forwards the session ID and partition key when the output
leaves the session ID `None`. The message ID, correlation ID, subject, content
type, time to live, and schedule are never inherited.
`without_application_properties()` disables property inheritance.

A handler that returns a plain value between a Service Bus source and sink gets
`ServiceBusInherit::new()` automatically. See the
[runtime guide](../runtime/handlers.md#handler-shapes). Register `TraceContext` after
`ServiceBusInherit` to replace inherited trace-context properties; the source
reads trace context from string application properties.

## Dead letters

`ServiceBusPublish::from_dead_letter` forwards a dead letter with its original
body, application properties, and message properties, and adds the failure
details and the entity path and sequence number of the first receipt as
`beavers-dlq-*` string application properties. It clears the message ID, so
duplicate detection on the dead-letter entity does not drop a payload
dead-lettered again, and the time to live, so the dead letter does not expire
with the original. `ServiceBusDeadLetter::from_record` reads the details back;
see [forwarding dead letters](../runtime/errors.md#forwarding-dead-letters-to-a-broker-topic).

Every queue and subscription also has a dead-letter subqueue, to which Service
Bus moves a message once its delivery count exceeds the entity's
`MaxDeliveryCount`. The subscription's error policy decides what happens to a
failed delivery first, so the subqueue receives messages that are delivered
again and again without being settled, for example because they crash the
process every time. Keep `MaxDeliveryCount` high enough for that. A source can
receive from the subqueue by its path, such as `orders/$DeadLetterQueue`.

## Delivery guarantees

A source ACK and a sink publication are separate operations, so a failure
between them, or a lock lost before the completion arrives, can produce a
duplicate. Service Bus pipelines are at-least-once; duplicate detection on the
target entity drops a repeated message ID only within its detection window.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/adapters/http.md -->

# HTTP adapter

The HTTP adapter connects pipelines to services whose interface is HTTP. Enable
it with the `http` feature:

```toml
[dependencies]
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["http"] }
```

- [`HttpSource`](#source) runs an HTTP/1.1 server and turns each `POST` request
  into a delivery. The response waits for the delivery's outcome, so a client
  learns whether its request was processed and can retry when it was not.
- [`HttpSink`](#sink) sends each output as an HTTP request and succeeds on a
  `2xx` response, so the input is acknowledged only after the destination
  accepted every output.

## Source

```rust,no_run
use beavers::{
    App, Json, Result, StdoutSink,
    adapters::http::{HttpRecord, HttpSource},
};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Order {
    id: u64,
}

async fn accept(record: HttpRecord<Order>) -> Result<Order> {
    Ok(record.body)
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let source = HttpSource::<Json<Order>>::new("0.0.0.0:8080".parse()?)?;
    App::new()
        .subscribe("orders", source, StdoutSink::<Json<_>>::new(), accept)
        .run()
        .await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

```sh
curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/orders -d '{"id":7}'
```

### Server configuration

The HTTP source has no shared handle; each source is its own server.

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `bind` | required | Listen address passed to `new`. Port 0 selects a free port. |
| `max_body_bytes(n)` | 1 MiB | Larger bodies are answered with `413` and never become deliveries. |
| `response(timing)` | `ResponseTiming::Ack` | When a received request is answered; see [response timing](#response-timing). |

`HttpSource::new(bind)` binds the listener immediately, so an address in use is
reported by the constructor and `local_addr()` returns the bound address,
including a port chosen for port 0. `HttpSource::with_codec(codec, bind)`
accepts a configured codec. `validate` checks the settings, and the server
validates them again when it starts accepting connections on the first
`receive`.

```rust,no_run
use beavers::{Utf8, adapters::http::{HttpSource, ResponseTiming}};

let source = HttpSource::<Utf8>::new("0.0.0.0:8080".parse()?)?
    .max_body_bytes(64 * 1024)
    .response(ResponseTiming::Receive);
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

### Records

Handlers receive `HttpRecord<T>`:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `path` | Request path, such as `/orders` |
| `query` | Query string without `?`, or `None` |
| `headers` | Lowercase names and byte values, one entry per received value |
| `body` | Body decoded by the source codec |
| `metadata.remote_addr` | Peer address of the TCP connection |

`header(name)` returns the first value of a header, matched case-insensitively.
Behind a reverse proxy, `remote_addr` is the proxy; forwarding headers such as
`X-Forwarded-For` remain in `headers`. The source accepts every path; a handler
or middleware that serves only some paths rejects the others.

The raw form carried by dead letters is `HttpRecord<Vec<u8>>` with the
undecoded body. Header values that are valid UTF-8, including `traceparent`,
are the delivery's propagation fields, so with the `opentelemetry` feature the
delivery span continues the client's trace.

### Decoding

The server decodes each body with the source codec as soon as the request is
read, before the request becomes a delivery. A body that fails to decode is
answered with `400 Bad Request` and the codec error as a plain-text body. It
never reaches the subscription, so the [error policy](../runtime/errors.md#error-policy)
and dead-letter sink do not see it, and one malformed request cannot stop the
subscription. `SourceMessage::decode` of an HTTP delivery therefore always
succeeds.

### Responses and delivery

With the default `ResponseTiming::Ack`, the server answers each decoded request
once its delivery has an outcome:

| Outcome | Status |
|---|---|
| ACK after processing, dead-lettering, or discarding | `200 OK` |
| Delivery dropped without ACK: subscription failure, shutdown, or drain timeout | `503 Service Unavailable` |
| Request not yet received when the subscription stops receiving | `503 Service Unavailable` |
| Body that fails to decode | `400 Bad Request` with the codec error |
| Method other than `POST` | `405 Method Not Allowed` |
| Body larger than `max_body_bytes` | `413 Payload Too Large` |
| Body not readable, such as an aborted upload | `400 Bad Request` |

A success status therefore means the subscription took responsibility for the
request: its outputs were published, or the error policy dead-lettered or
intentionally discarded it. A client that retries on `503`, on a timeout, and on
a closed connection gets at-least-once processing. Its retry can duplicate a
request whose response was lost, so outputs should tolerate duplicates.

A client that disconnects while its request is processed does not cancel the
delivery. The delivery is acknowledged normally and the response is dropped.

Handler rejections are dead-lettered by default and then answered with `200`;
without a dead-letter sink they stop the subscription, and the server with it.

### Response timing

`ResponseTiming::Receive` answers `202 Accepted` as soon as the subscription
receives the decoded request, before processing. Clients get a response
without waiting for the pipeline, but a success status no longer means the
request was processed:

- A request is lost if the process stops before its delivery completes.
- Handler and publish failures are not reported to the client, so configure the
  error policy and a dead-letter sink to keep them.
- Requests not yet received when the subscription stops receiving are still
  answered with `503`, and invalid or undecodable requests still receive `405`,
  `413`, or `400` before they become deliveries.

Use it when the producer cannot wait for processing and occasional loss on a
crash is acceptable. Keep the default when every accepted request must be
processed at least once.

### Backpressure and ordering

Requests wait in a queue of one until the subscription receives them, so a
subscription at its `max_in_flight` limit makes new requests wait instead of
failing. Clients should apply a timeout. Requests have no ordering key; with
`concurrency` above one they are processed in parallel and complete in any
order.

### Closing

When the subscription stops receiving, on application shutdown or a failure,
the runtime calls `stop_receiving` before draining. The source then stops
accepting connections, closes idle keep-alive connections, and answers queued
requests that were not received with `503`. New connections are refused while
received requests drain; their connections stay open until each delivery
completes and its response is sent.

`close` runs after draining, within the drain timeout. It does the same and
then waits until open connections have answered their current request.
Dropping the source also stops the listener.

Behind a load balancer, serve [health checks](../runtime/health.md)
with the `health` feature. Readiness fails as soon as shutdown starts, so a
Kubernetes Service stops routing new requests to an instance before its source
refuses them.

### Server metrics

The server records these metrics through the `metrics` facade, alongside the
[subscription metrics](../runtime/observability.md). Each carries a `listener`
label with the bound address.

| Metric | Type | Extra labels | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `beavers_http_requests_total` | counter | `status` | Answered requests by response status |
| `beavers_http_request_duration_seconds` | histogram | `status` | Time from receiving the request head to the response |
| `beavers_http_requests_in_flight` | gauge | | Requests being read, decoded, or awaiting their delivery |
| `beavers_http_connections_open` | gauge | | Open client connections |
| `beavers_http_request_body_bytes` | histogram | | Size of bodies read within `max_body_bytes` |

A request whose client disconnects before the response is not counted in
`beavers_http_requests_total`. Decode failures appear as `status="400"` and
never reach the subscription's `beavers_delivery_failures_total`.

### Server limitations

- HTTP/1.1 only, without TLS. Terminate TLS and HTTP/2 at a reverse proxy.
- Responses have no body. Returning handler output to the client, as a
  request-reply endpoint, is not supported.
- No request timeout is enforced by the server; the drain timeout bounds how
  long shutdown waits for open requests.

## Sink

`HttpSink<C>` accepts `HttpPublish<T>` outputs, where `T` is the codec's value type. It encodes each body with
its codec and sends one request per output to its URL. A typical use
is handing events consumed from a broker to a service with an HTTP API:

```rust,ignore
use beavers::{
    App, Json, Result,
    adapters::{
        http::{HttpClient, HttpPublish},
        kafka::{Kafka, KafkaRecord},
    },
};

async fn to_request(record: KafkaRecord<Order>) -> Result<HttpPublish<Order>> {
    let metadata = record.metadata.clone();
    let order = record.value.ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("tombstone"))?;
    // A stable key lets the service recognize a redelivered event.
    let key = format!("{}-{}-{}", metadata.topic, metadata.partition, metadata.offset);
    Ok(HttpPublish::new(order).with_header("idempotency-key", key))
}

let source = Kafka::new("localhost:9092").source::<Json<Order>>("orders-to-billing", ["orders"]);
let sink = HttpClient::new()
    .sink::<Json<Order>>("https://billing.internal/orders")
    .header("content-type", "application/json");
App::new().subscribe("orders", source, sink, to_request).run().await?;
```

### Sink configuration

An `HttpClient` handle holds the settings and the connection pool that the
sinks built from it share. Its sinks send through one pool per handle, which
keeps idle connections to each destination for reuse. The handle creates
separate pools for `http` and `https` destinations, each on its first request,
and loads the platform's root certificates only for the `https` pool. Idle
connections close once the handle and every sink built from it have been
dropped. Each handle builder method returns a handle with a pool of its own, so
configure the handle before building sinks from it. The `Debug` output of the
handle shows header names only.

| Handle method | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `header(name, value)` | none | Header sent with every request of every sink, such as `authorization` |
| `timeout(duration)` | 30 s | Limit for one attempt, from connecting until the response body is read, for sinks that set none |

`sink::<C>(url)` builds a sink with the codec's default value, and
`sink_with_codec(codec, url)` with a configured codec. The URL is required; the
other settings are sink builder methods:

| Sink setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `url` | required | Absolute `http` or `https` URL, including any path and query |
| `method(method)` | `HttpMethod::Post` | `Post`, `Put`, or `Patch` |
| `header(name, value)` | handle headers | Header sent with every request, such as `content-type`; replaces the handle's headers of the same name |
| `timeout(duration)` | handle timeout | Limit for one attempt, replacing the handle's timeout |

```rust
use beavers::{Json, adapters::http::{HttpClient, HttpMethod}};
use std::time::Duration;

let http = HttpClient::new()
    .header("authorization", "Bearer token")
    .timeout(Duration::from_secs(10));
let orders = http
    .sink::<Json<String>>("https://billing.example.com/orders")
    .header("content-type", "application/json");
let refunds = http
    .sink::<Json<String>>("https://billing.example.com/refunds")
    .method(HttpMethod::Put)
    .timeout(Duration::from_secs(60));
```

The handle and the sink each have `validate`. The sink's returns an error for a
URL without a host, a scheme other than `http` or `https`, credentials in the
URL, invalid header names or values, or a zero timeout, and the sink validates
its settings again when it prepares its first output. Clones of a sink share
its closing state.

`https` servers are verified against the platform's root certificates; a
platform without any fails every `https` publication. The codec does not set
`content-type`, so set it with `header`.

### Requests

`HttpPublish<T>` carries the body and optional `headers`. A header name set on
an output replaces every handle and sink header of that name; repeating a name on
the output sends each value. Header names are case-insensitive, and invalid
names or values fail `prepare`, which the error policy routes as `Encode`. The
prepared request keeps the encoded body and complete header set, so a retry
sends the same bytes without encoding again.

`HttpPublish` implements `PropagationCarrier`, so with the `opentelemetry`
feature the outgoing request carries the delivery's `traceparent` header.
HTTP records have no tombstones, so `HttpPublish` does not implement
`TombstonePublish`, and `Tombstones` middleware for an HTTP sink does not
compile.

### Responses and retries

Each output waits for its response before the next output of the delivery is
sent, and the delivery is acknowledged after every output succeeded:

| Result | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `2xx` | Published |
| `408`, `429`, or `5xx` | Retried under `publish_retry` |
| Connection failure or `timeout` | Retried under `publish_retry` |
| Any other status, including `3xx` redirects | [`PublishRejected`](../runtime/errors.md#error-policy) without retry |

An exhausted retry stops the subscription without ACK, so a destination that is
down leaves the input unacknowledged for redelivery after restart. A rejected
output is routed by the error policy as `FailureKind::PublishRejected`, which
dead-letters the input by default and stops the subscription when no
dead-letter sink is configured. The error text names the method, URL without
its query, status, and the start of the response body.

Delivery is at-least-once. A request whose response is lost or times out is
sent again, the whole delivery is processed again after a crash or a failure of
a later output, and outputs published before a rejection stay published. The
destination should treat requests as idempotent, for example by keying them on
the source record's position, as the example does. Redirects are not followed
and `Retry-After` is not honored; retry delays come from `publish_retry`.

Outputs of one delivery are sent in order. Deliveries processed concurrently
send their requests concurrently over pooled HTTP/1.1 connections, so the
subscription's `concurrency` bounds the requests in flight to one destination.

### Closing the sink

`close` only refuses further publications from the sink and all its clones.
Requests already in progress finish, and the handle's connection pool stays
open for its other sinks.

### Client metrics

Each attempt is recorded through the `metrics` facade with a `url` label
holding the scheme, host, and path, without the query, and an `outcome` label
holding the response status, `error` for a failed connection or response, or
`timeout`.

| Metric | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `beavers_http_client_requests_total` | counter | Request attempts, including retried ones |
| `beavers_http_client_request_duration_seconds` | histogram | Time from sending the request to reading the response body |

### Sink limitations

- HTTP/1.1 only. Client certificates and custom root certificates are not
  configurable.
- The URL and method are fixed per sink; an output cannot choose its path.
- Response bodies are discarded after success and truncated in error messages.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/json.md -->

# JSON codec

`Json<T>` converts between JSON payloads and a type `T` implementing Serde's
traits. It holds no state, implements `Default` for every `T`, and is always
available; it needs no Cargo feature. Decode into `serde_json::Value` when the
payload has no fixed schema; see [JSON without a schema](#json-without-a-schema).

`Json` uses `serde_json::from_slice` for decoding and `serde_json::to_vec` for
encoding.

| Operation | Payload requirement | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Decode | `serde::de::DeserializeOwned` | Owned typed value |
| Encode | `serde::Serialize` | Compact JSON bytes |

Json does not itself append a newline or split a stream into messages. Input
framing belongs to the source; output framing belongs to the sink. In particular,
StdinSource reads one line at a time and StdoutSink appends a newline after encoding.

## Using JSON with adapters

Select the codec through the adapter's type parameter. The handler determines
the input and output payload types:

```rust
use beavers::{App, Json, Result, StdinSource, StdoutSink};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Deserialize)]
struct Order {
    id: u64,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Event {
    order_id: u64,
}

async fn handler(order: Order) -> Result<Event> {
    Ok(Event { order_id: order.id })
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    App::new()
        .subscribe(
            "orders",
            StdinSource::<Json<_>>::new(),
            StdoutSink::<Json<_>>::new(),
            handler,
        )
        .run()
        .await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

The `_` in `Json<_>` is the payload type, inferred here from the handler as
`Order` for the source and `Event` for the sink. Input values also need the runtime's `Clone + Send + Sync + 'static`
bounds; those are not additional requirements of the JSON format.

The [transform example](https://github.com/cafeal/beave-rs/blob/main/examples/transform.rs) provides this pipeline. Feed it
one order object per line:

```sh
printf '%s\n' '{"id":10}' '{"id":20}' | cargo run --example transform -- --stdin
```

IterSource and InMemorySink already exchange typed values, so they require no
serialization codec.

## JSON without a schema

When payloads have no fixed shape, decode into `serde_json::Value` and read the
fields the handler needs. Any valid JSON decodes; only malformed JSON is a
decode failure. Import `Value` so the codec type stays short:

```rust,ignore
use beavers::{App, Json, Result, StdoutSink, adapters::kafka::Kafka};
use serde_json::Value;

async fn audit(event: Value) -> Result<Value> {
    let kind = event["type"].as_str().unwrap_or("unknown");
    Ok(serde_json::json!({ "type": kind }))
}

let kafka = Kafka::new("localhost:9092");
App::new()
    .subscribe(
        "audit",
        kafka.source::<Json<Value>>("audit", ["events"]),
        StdoutSink::<Json<Value>>::new(),
        audit,
    )
    .run()
    .await?;
```

A `Json<Value>` sink accepts any `Value`, so a handler can also build output
with `serde_json::json!` without declaring a struct.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/raw-bytes.md -->

# Raw bytes codec

`RawBytes` decodes a byte slice to `Vec<u8>` and encodes a `Vec<u8>` to bytes.
It copies the payload without interpreting it. Empty payloads and every byte
value are valid, including zero bytes and malformed UTF-8. It is a unit struct
that implements `Default`, so adapters that construct their codec internally
can use it, and it needs no Cargo feature. Its value type is fixed, so a source
or sink names it without a type argument, as in `KafkaSink<RawBytes>`.

```rust
use beavers::{Decoder, Encoder, RawBytes};

let codec = RawBytes;
let value = codec.decode(&[0, 0xff, b'\n'])?;
assert_eq!(codec.encode(&value)?, vec![0, 0xff, b'\n']);
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

Framing remains the adapter's responsibility. A line-based source may remove
or preserve delimiters according to its own contract, and a sink may append
delimiters after encoding. `RawBytes` does not change framing on its own. For
payloads that must be valid text, use [`Utf8`](utf8.md).

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/utf8.md -->

# UTF-8 codec

`Utf8` decodes bytes to `String` only when the complete payload is valid UTF-8,
and encodes a `String` using its UTF-8 representation. It does not trim text,
strip a byte-order mark, normalize Unicode, or remove line endings. An empty
payload decodes to an empty string. Malformed UTF-8 returns an error. It is a
unit struct that implements `Default`, so adapters that construct their codec
internally can use it, and it needs no Cargo feature. Its value type is fixed,
so a source or sink names it without a type argument, as in `KafkaSink<Utf8>`.

```rust
use beavers::{Decoder, Encoder, Utf8};

let codec = Utf8;
let value = codec.decode("hello\n".as_bytes())?;
assert_eq!(value, "hello\n");
assert_eq!(codec.encode(&value)?, b"hello\n");
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

Framing remains the adapter's responsibility. A line-based source may remove
or preserve delimiters according to its own contract, and a sink may append
delimiters after encoding. `Utf8` does not change framing on its own. For
arbitrary bytes, use [`RawBytes`](raw-bytes.md).

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/protobuf.md -->

# Protobuf codec

`Protobuf<T>` encodes and decodes a type `T` implementing [`prost::Message`]. Enable
the `protobuf` Cargo feature to use it:

```toml
[dependencies]
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["protobuf"] }
```

The codec passes raw Protocol Buffers message bytes through. Encoding calls
`prost::Message::encode_to_vec`; decoding calls `prost::Message::decode`, so
malformed or truncated payloads return an error. An empty message encodes to an
empty payload and an empty payload decodes to the message's `Default` value.

```rust
use beavers::{Decoder, Encoder, Protobuf};

// `Event` is a type generated by prost (or derives `prost::Message`).
let codec = Protobuf::<Event>::new();
let bytes = codec.encode(&event)?;
let decoded = codec.decode(&bytes)?;
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

`Protobuf` does not add a length delimiter, envelope, or other framing. The
adapter is responsible for preserving message boundaries, and the same bytes
can be exchanged directly with prost's `encode_to_vec` and `decode` methods.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/avro.md -->

# Avro codec

`Avro` encodes and decodes Serde values using a parsed Apache Avro schema. Enable
the `avro` Cargo feature:

```toml
[dependencies]
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["avro"] }
```

Construct the codec with a schema string. Construction parses and validates the
schema once; an invalid schema returns an error before any messages are handled.
The same schema is used as the writer and reader schema for the codec:

```rust
use beavers::{Avro, Decoder, Encoder};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

const SCHEMA: &str = r#"
{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Order",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "id", "type": "long"},
    {"name": "comment", "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}
  ]
}
"#;

#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Order {
    id: i64,
    comment: Option<String>,
}

let codec = Avro::new(SCHEMA)?;
let bytes = codec.encode(&Order { id: 7, comment: None })?;
let order: Order = codec.decode(&bytes)?;
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

Each payload is exactly one raw Avro datum. `Avro` does not add an object
container header, sync marker, length prefix, or other framing. A decode succeeds
only when the schema consumes the complete payload; trailing bytes are rejected.
This makes the codec suitable for adapters that already preserve message
boundaries. It is directly compatible with Apache Avro's
`GenericDatumWriter`/`GenericDatumReader` APIs.

Serde types must match the schema's Avro data model. Records map to structs,
unit enums map to Avro enums, `Option<T>` maps to a nullable union, and `Vec<T>`
maps to an array. For Avro `bytes` and `fixed`, use the byte helper modules
documented by `apache-avro` when deriving Serde implementations.

The codec intentionally has no `Default` implementation because a schema is
required. Pass an instance to an adapter that accepts an existing codec, such
as `kafka.source_with_codec(codec, group_id, topics)`,
`kafka.sink_with_codec(codec, topic)`, or `StdoutSink::with_codec(codec)`.

Schema evolution is not implicit: this API has no separate reader schema. If a
producer and consumer use different schemas, create a codec with the producer's
schema only when they are known to be compatible, or use Apache Avro's datum
reader directly with explicit writer and reader schemas.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/msgpack.md -->

# MessagePack codec

`MessagePack<T>` converts between [MessagePack](https://msgpack.org/) payloads
and a type `T` implementing Serde's traits, the same types `Json` accepts. It
holds no state and implements `Default`. Enable the `msgpack` Cargo feature to
use it:

```toml
[dependencies]
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["msgpack"] }
```

Encoding calls `rmp_serde::to_vec_named`; decoding reads the complete payload
with `rmp_serde`.

```rust
use beavers::{Decoder, Encoder, MessagePack};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Order {
    id: u64,
}

let bytes = MessagePack::new().encode(&Order { id: 42 })?;
let order: Order = MessagePack::new().decode(&bytes)?;
assert_eq!(order, Order { id: 42 });
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

## Struct representation

`MessagePack` encodes a struct as a map keyed by field name rather than as a
positional array. Payloads are larger than the array form, but other
MessagePack implementations can read them by name, and a reader tolerates
fields that were added, removed, or reordered, as with JSON. Decoding also
accepts the array form that `rmp_serde::to_vec` writes.

## Failures and framing

Decoding rejects malformed or truncated input and payloads that contain bytes
after the first value, so one payload cannot silently carry more than one value.
These are decode failures; see [lifecycle and failures](../codecs.md#lifecycle-and-failures).

`MessagePack` adds no framing. Its output is binary and can contain newline
bytes, so it does not suit line-based adapters such as `StdinSource`, and
brokers whose bodies carry text only, such as SQS, need the
[`Base64` wrapper](wrappers/base64.md).

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/cbor.md -->

# CBOR codec

`Cbor` converts between CBOR ([RFC 8949](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949))
payloads and a type `T` implementing Serde's traits, the same types `Json`
accepts. `Cbor<T>` holds no state and implements `Default`. Enable the `cbor` Cargo
feature to use it:

```toml
[dependencies]
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["cbor"] }
```

Encoding calls `ciborium::into_writer`; decoding calls `ciborium::from_reader`
over the complete payload.

```rust
use beavers::{Cbor, Decoder, Encoder};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Reading {
    sensor: String,
}

let bytes = Cbor::new().encode(&Reading { sensor: "dam-1".into() })?;
let reading: Reading = Cbor::new().decode(&bytes)?;
assert_eq!(reading.sensor, "dam-1");
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

## Representation

`Cbor` writes the representation `ciborium` chooses for each Serde type: a
struct is a map keyed by field name, and `Vec<u8>` is an array of integers
unless the field uses a byte-string helper such as `serde_bytes`. It does not
write a self-describe tag, CBOR sequences, or COSE structures.

## Failures and framing

Decoding rejects malformed or truncated input and payloads that contain bytes
after the first value, so one payload cannot silently carry more than one value.
These are decode failures; see [lifecycle and failures](../codecs.md#lifecycle-and-failures).

`Cbor` adds no framing. Its output is binary and can contain newline bytes, so
it does not suit line-based adapters such as `StdinSource`, and brokers whose
bodies carry text only, such as SQS, need the
[`Base64` wrapper](wrappers/base64.md).

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/wrappers.md -->

# Codec wrappers

`Base64<C>`, `Gzip<C>`, and `Zstd<C>` wrap another codec `C` and transform its
payload. Encoding runs the inner codec first and then the wrapper; decoding runs
the wrapper first and passes its output to the inner codec. They accept any
inner codec, including other wrappers, and implement `Decoder` or
`Encoder` whenever the inner codec does, with the inner codec's value type.

| Wrapper | Cargo feature | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| [`Base64<C>`](wrappers/base64.md) | `base64` | Standard Base64 text of the inner payload |
| [`Gzip<C>`](wrappers/gzip.md) | `gzip` | One gzip member containing the inner payload |
| [`Zstd<C>`](wrappers/zstd.md) | `zstd` | One Zstandard frame containing the inner payload |

Each wrapper implements `Default` when its inner codec does, so it works with
adapters that construct their codec with `C::default()`. Use the adapter
handle's `source_with_codec` or `sink_with_codec` to pass a wrapper with
non-default settings or a configured inner codec such as `Avro`.

```rust,ignore
use beavers::adapters::sqs::Sqs;
use beavers::{Base64, Gzip, Protobuf};

// Protobuf bytes, gzip-compressed, carried as text in an SQS body.
let sink = Sqs::new().sink::<Base64<Gzip<Protobuf<Event>>>>(queue_url);
```

The order of nested wrappers is the order of the encoding steps from the inside
out: `Base64<Gzip<Json>>` compresses JSON and then encodes the compressed bytes
as Base64. The reader of the payload must use the same nesting.

Wrappers do not record what they did in the payload or in message metadata. A
decoder therefore expects every payload in a stream to use the same wrapping;
a subscription that receives both compressed and uncompressed payloads needs a
custom codec that tells them apart.

## Choosing compression

Gzip is readable by almost every platform; Zstandard compresses better and
faster where both ends support it. Both decompress into memory and fail to
decode once the output would exceed `with_max_decoded_len`, 64 MiB by default,
so a small, highly compressible payload cannot exhaust memory.

On Kafka, prefer the producer's batch compression: set the librdkafka
`compression.type` property, such as `zstd`, with `Kafka::producer_property`,
and consumers decompress transparently. Batch compression sees repeated
content across records and keeps payloads readable by any Kafka client. The
Pulsar sink does not expose producer compression yet. The compression wrappers
suit brokers without built-in compression, such as SQS, Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ, and
Azure Service Bus, and payloads that must stay compressed end to end.
Compressed payloads are binary, so SQS also needs `Base64` around them.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/wrappers/base64.md -->

# Base64 wrapper

`Base64<C>` carries the payload of an inner codec `C` as Base64 text. Enable
the `base64` Cargo feature to use it:

```toml
[dependencies]
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["base64"] }
```

Encoding runs the inner codec and encodes its output with the standard alphabet
and padding from
[RFC 4648, section 4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4648#section-4).
Decoding accepts exactly that form: whitespace, line breaks, missing padding,
and the URL-safe alphabet are errors. The output is ASCII, which makes binary
codecs usable where bodies carry text only, such as [SQS](../../adapters/sqs.md)
bodies.

```rust
use beavers::{Base64, Decoder, Encoder, RawBytes};

let codec = Base64::new(RawBytes);
assert_eq!(codec.encode(&vec![0xfb, 0xff])?, b"+/8=");
assert_eq!(codec.decode(b"+/8=")?, vec![0xfb, 0xff]);
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

`Base64::new(inner)` wraps a configured codec, and `Base64::default()` wraps
`C::default()`. See [codec wrappers](../wrappers.md) for nesting and use with
adapters.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/wrappers/gzip.md -->

# Gzip wrapper

`Gzip<C>` compresses the payload of an inner codec `C` as gzip
([RFC 1952](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1952)) through `flate2`. Enable
the `gzip` Cargo feature to use it:

```toml
[dependencies]
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["gzip"] }
```

Encoding runs the inner codec and writes its output as one gzip member.
Decoding decompresses every concatenated member and passes the result to the
inner codec, so payloads from other gzip writers decode as well.

| Setting | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| `with_level` | 6 | 0 (store only) to 9 (smallest output) |
| `with_max_decoded_len` | 64 MiB | Any byte count |

```rust
use beavers::{Decoder, Encoder, Gzip, Json};

let codec = Gzip::new(Json::new()).with_level(9);
let bytes = codec.encode(&vec!["beaver"; 100])?;
let value: Vec<String> = codec.decode(&bytes)?;
assert_eq!(value.len(), 100);
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

`with_level` panics on a level above 9, because the value is fixed when the
codec is constructed. Decoding fails when the decompressed payload would exceed
`with_max_decoded_len`, and malformed compressed data is also a decode failure.
See [codec wrappers](../wrappers.md#choosing-compression) for when to compress
in the codec rather than in the broker client.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/codecs/wrappers/zstd.md -->

# Zstd wrapper

`Zstd<C>` compresses the payload of an inner codec `C` as Zstandard
([RFC 8878](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8878)) through the `zstd` crate,
which compiles the reference C library. Enable the `zstd` Cargo feature to use
it:

```toml
[dependencies]
beavers = { version = "0.1", features = ["zstd"] }
```

Encoding runs the inner codec and writes its output as one Zstandard frame.
Decoding decompresses every concatenated frame and passes the result to the
inner codec, so payloads from other Zstandard writers decode as well.

| Setting | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| `with_level` | 3 | Negative levels for speed up to 22; the linked library's range |
| `with_max_decoded_len` | 64 MiB | Any byte count |

```rust
use beavers::{Decoder, Encoder, Json, Zstd};

let codec = Zstd::new(Json::new())
    .with_level(9)
    .with_max_decoded_len(1024 * 1024);
let bytes = codec.encode(&vec!["beaver"; 100])?;
let value: Vec<String> = codec.decode(&bytes)?;
assert_eq!(value.len(), 100);
# Ok::<(), beavers::BoxError>(())
```

`with_level` panics on a level outside the library's range, because the value
is fixed when the codec is constructed. Decoding fails when the decompressed
payload would exceed `with_max_decoded_len`, and malformed compressed data is
also a decode failure. See
[codec wrappers](../wrappers.md#choosing-compression) for when to compress in
the codec rather than in the broker client.

<!-- https://cafeal.github.io/beave-rs/pr-preview/pr-56/docs/development.md -->

# Local development brokers

`compose.yaml` at the repository root starts single-node Kafka, Apache Pulsar,
and RabbitMQ brokers, an ElasticMQ SQS emulator, the Google Cloud Pub/Sub
emulator, and the Azure Service Bus emulator, with web consoles for the
brokers. Use it to run the broker examples, the
ignored live tests, and manual experiments. It requires Docker with Compose v2.

## Quick start

```sh
docker compose up -d --wait   # start the brokers and wait until they are healthy
cargo kafka-produce           # publish sample orders to Kafka
cargo kafka-process           # run the Kafka pipeline until Ctrl-C
cargo test-live               # run every ignored live test
docker compose down           # stop the brokers and discard their data
```

The `cargo` commands are aliases defined in `.cargo/config.toml`; they only
run `cargo run --example` and `cargo test` with the required features. Cargo
aliases cannot start Docker, so the brokers are always started and stopped with
`docker compose` directly.

## Managing the environment

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `docker compose up -d --wait` | Starts every service and returns when the brokers pass their health checks |
| `docker compose up -d --wait kafka pulsar rabbitmq elasticmq pubsub servicebus-health` | Starts only the brokers, without the separate web consoles; `servicebus-health` brings the Service Bus emulator and its SQL Server |
| `docker compose ps --all` | Shows the state of each service, including the finished `pulsar-init` |
| `docker compose logs -f pulsar` | Follows the logs of one service |
| `docker compose down` | Stops and removes the containers |

The brokers keep no named volumes, so `docker compose down` discards every
topic, offset, and subscription; the next `up` starts from empty brokers.
`docker compose stop` keeps the containers and their data for a later
`docker compose start`.

## Services

| Service | Address | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Kafka | `localhost:9092` | Kafka 4.1 in KRaft mode |
| Kafka UI | <http://localhost:8081> | Topics, messages, and consumer groups (kafbat kafka-ui) |
| Pulsar | `pulsar://localhost:6650` | Pulsar 4.0 standalone |
| Pulsar admin API | <http://localhost:8080> | `pulsar-admin --admin-url` and REST |
| Pulsar Manager | <http://localhost:9527> | Tenants, topics, and subscriptions; log in as `admin` / `apachepulsar` |
| RabbitMQ | `amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/%2f` | RabbitMQ 4.1 |
| RabbitMQ management | <http://localhost:15672> | Queues, exchanges, connections, and the management HTTP API; log in as `guest` / `guest` |
| ElasticMQ | <http://localhost:9324> | SQS-compatible API; queue URLs look like `http://localhost:9324/000000000000/orders` |
| ElasticMQ UI | <http://localhost:9325> | Queues and their message counts |
| Pub/Sub emulator | `localhost:8085` | Pub/Sub gRPC and REST APIs for the `beavers` project; set the adapter `endpoint` to `http://localhost:8085` |
| Service Bus emulator | `localhost:5673` | Azure Service Bus over plain AMQP; connection string `Endpoint=sb://localhost:5673;SharedAccessKeyName=RootManageSharedAccessKey;SharedAccessKey=SAS_KEY_VALUE;UseDevelopmentEmulator=true` |
| Service Bus emulator management | <http://localhost:5300> | Health endpoint and the queue management API the live tests use |

The examples and live tests use these addresses by default. Set these
variables to target other brokers:

| Variable | Default | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `KAFKA_BROKERS` | `localhost:9092` | Kafka examples and live tests |
| `PULSAR_URL` | `pulsar://localhost:6650` in examples, `pulsar://127.0.0.1:6650` in tests | Pulsar examples and live tests |
| `HTTP_SINK_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:8090/orders` | `kafka_to_http` example |
| `PULSAR_ADMIN_ADDR` | `127.0.0.1:8080` | Live tests that create Pulsar topics or subscriptions |
| `RABBITMQ_URL` | `amqp://guest:guest@127.0.0.1:5672/%2f` | RabbitMQ live tests |
| `RABBITMQ_MANAGEMENT_ADDR` | `127.0.0.1:15672` | RabbitMQ live tests that declare queues or close connections |
| `SQS_ENDPOINT` | `http://127.0.0.1:9324` | SQS live tests |
| `PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST` | `127.0.0.1:8085` | Pub/Sub live tests |
| `SERVICEBUS_CONNECTION_STRING` | The emulator connection string on `127.0.0.1:5673` | Service Bus live tests |
| `SERVICEBUS_ADMIN_ADDR` | `127.0.0.1:5300` | Service Bus live tests that create or delete queues |

## Broker configuration

Kafka auto-creates topics with three partitions, so per-partition ordering and
parallelism are visible with a single broker. Replication factors are 1 and the
transaction state log accepts a single replica, which allows transactional
producers against the one broker. Applications on the host use the listener
advertised as `localhost:9092`; containers use `kafka:29092`.

Pulsar runs in standalone mode without the functions worker or stream storage.
`standalone.conf` settings can be added to the `pulsar` service environment, which `apply-config-from-env.py`
applies before the broker starts.

The one-shot `pulsar-init` service runs after the broker and Pulsar Manager
start. It creates the `beavers-examples` subscription on
`persistent://public/default/orders` at the earliest position, because a new
Pulsar subscription otherwise starts at the latest message, and it creates the
Pulsar Manager login. Pulsar Manager is preconfigured with a `local`
environment pointing at the broker. The credentials are for local use only.

RabbitMQ runs with its management plugin and the default `guest` user, which
the broker accepts from the host through the published port. It starts without
queues; the live tests declare their own through the management API.

ElasticMQ implements the SQS API in memory and accepts any credentials and
region. Point a handle at it with
`Sqs::new().region("elasticmq").endpoint_url("http://localhost:9324")` and
static credentials such as `.credentials(SqsCredentials::new("local", "local"))`.
It starts without queues; create one with the AWS CLI
(`aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9324 sqs create-queue --queue-name orders`)
or the query API, as the live tests do. It does not reproduce every AWS limit
and behavior, so verify production settings against SQS itself.

The Pub/Sub emulator, from the `google/cloud-sdk` emulators image, keeps topics
and subscriptions in memory and needs no credentials. Connect to it with
`PubSub::new().endpoint("http://localhost:8085").anonymous()`. It starts without topics; create them through
its REST API, as the live tests do:

```sh
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8085/v1/projects/beavers/topics/orders
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8085/v1/projects/beavers/subscriptions/orders \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"topic":"projects/beavers/topics/orders"}'
```

It does not reproduce every Pub/Sub limit and behavior, so verify production
settings against Pub/Sub itself.

The Service Bus emulator stores its entities in the `servicebus-sql` SQL Server
container and reads its namespace from `dev/servicebus/config.json`, which
defines the `beavers-events` topic with the `beavers-test` subscription.
Connect to it with `ServiceBus::from_connection_string(...)` and the connection
string listed above; `UseDevelopmentEmulator=true` selects plain AMQP, which
`.emulator()` sets on a handle built with `ServiceBus::new`. Its
management API on port 5300 creates and deletes queues
(`PUT /{queue}?api-version=2021-05` with an Atom `QueueDescription`), as the
live tests do, but cannot create topic subscriptions, so add topics and
subscriptions to the configuration file and recreate the container. Its AMQP
port is published as 5673 because RabbitMQ uses 5672. The emulator image has no
shell, so the `servicebus-health` container polls its health endpoint for
